docs.title: training_image_consistency builtin
docs.text:
training_image_consistency(
    ti,
    column,
    coords,
    values,
    *,
    grid=None,
    categorical=True,
    axis=None,
    pattern_length=4,
    n_classes=4,
    n_samples=200,
    seed=0,
)

How often the patterns of the hard data occur in a training image, after Boisvert, Pyrcz and Deutsch (2007); run it to reject an image before simulating with it.

The data are placed in the cells of grid, one per cell. Along axis, runs of consecutive informed cells (the holes) are cut into data events of pattern_length cells, and the frequencies of their patterns are compared with those of every run of pattern_length cells along the same axis of the image, by their Jensen-Shannon divergence: 0 for the same frequencies, 1 when no pattern is shared. Holes of the data's lengths are then drilled n_samples times through the image at random columns and depths and compared with it the same way; the p-value is the share of these reference divergences at least as large as the data's.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ti BlockModel

The training image, regular or masked; read one image cell per grid cell, as in a simulation.

required column str

Column of ti holding the image: integer codes 0 to 254 when categorical, else values.

required coords PointSet or array_like

The hard data, or their (n, 2) or (n, 3) coordinates, sampled at about the grid's cell size along axis.

required values array_like or str

Codes of the image (categorical) or values of the hard data, or their column in coords. Data without a value or outside grid are left out.

required grid BlockModel

The simulation grid; by default the geometry of ti.

None categorical bool

Compare codes; otherwise cut the values into n_classes classes.

True axis (x, y, z)

Axis the holes follow; by default "z" on a 3D grid, "y" on a 2D one.

"x" pattern_length int

Cells in a data event, at least 2. Longer patterns tell images apart better but need longer runs of data.

4 n_classes int

Continuous images only: classes cut at the quantiles of the hard data, 2 to 254.

4 n_samples int

Reference draws; the smallest p-value is 1 / (n_samples + 1).

200 seed int

The same seed gives the same result on any number of threads.

0

Returns:

Type Description dict

distance (the data's divergence from the image, 0 to 1), p_value (below 0.05, holes like the data seldom come from the image), reference (the reference divergences, ascending), unseen (share of the data events whose pattern the image lacks), n_events, n_cells (grid cells with data), and for categorical images proportions and data_proportions (share of each code in the image and in the data cells; None for continuous images).

Raises:

Type Description InvalidInput

If a data code is not a code of the image, an option is out of range, the grid or image is shorter than pattern_length along axis, or no hole has pattern_length consecutive informed cells.

Notes

Only one axis is compared: vertical holes test the thickness, order and proportions of the units, not the width or orientation of bodies.

Examples:

>>> check = cs.training_image_consistency(ti, "facies", holes, "facies", seed=0)
>>> check["p_value"]

docs.title: SNESIM
docs.text:
SNESIM (Strebelle, 2002): categories, or classes of values, simulated from the patterns of a training image.

The patterns around each cell of the image are counted once into search trees, one per multigrid level and template class, on simulate. A node reads the categories at the template_size cells nearest to it and draws its own from the image's counts of that data event. Patterns are read in cell index space, so the targets' cells match the image's cells one to one, unless simulate turns or stretches them with local anisotropy.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ti BlockModel or dict

Regular or masked training image; null and masked-out cells are not patterns. A dict {domain: (model, column)} gives each domain its own image, picked by domains or domain_column in simulate; the images share one code set, 0 to the largest code of any of them.

required column str

Column of ti holding category codes, integers 0 to 254; required with one image, left out with a dict.

required template_size int

Cells every node reads, nearest first.

40 n_levels int

Coarse grids above the finest, at spacings 2^L; half of the template of a coarse level stays next to the node, where it sees hard data, the rest spreads over the level's grid. 0 uses the finest grid only.

3 min_replicates int

Fewest replicates of a data event in the image; the farthest informed cells are dropped until enough remain, down to the image's proportions.

10 target_proportions sequence of float

Proportion of each code 0..k, summing to 1, that a servosystem steers each realization towards.

required servo float

Servosystem strength in [0, 1): a node draws from P(c) + servo / (1 - servo) * (target(c) - current(c)); 0 switches it off.

0.5 angle_step float

Degrees the local angles of simulate's anisotropy are rounded to; the logarithm of each affinity is rounded to angle_step in radians (factors about 1.19 apart at 10), so that either rounding moves a template cell at distance r by about r * angle_step. Each distinct rounded (image, angles, affinity) is a template class with search trees of its own; a wider step makes fewer.

10.0 categorical bool

Whether column holds codes or continuous values. By default it is categorical when every value is an integer from 0 to 254.

required cutoffs sequence of float

Strictly ascending values cutting a continuous image into classes, which SNESIM simulates as categories. Each simulated cell then takes the value of a cell of its image in its class: of 32 drawn at random, the one whose 8 nearest neighbors best match the values already simulated around it. By default the quartiles of the image's values; few classes keep the patterns frequent enough to count. Ignored for a categorical image.

required

Examples:

>>> grid = cs.BlockModel((0, 0), (1, 1), (80, 80))
>>> ti = cs.object_training_image(
...     grid,
...     [{"shape": "channel", "code": 1, "proportion": 0.3, "width": 6,
...       "azimuth": (80, 100), "amplitude": 6, "wavelength": 50}],
... )
>>> summary = cs.SNESIM(ti, "facies", template_size=24).simulate(grid, n=4)

docs.text:
simulate(
    targets,
    *,
    n=100,
    seed=0,
    keep=None,
    soft=None,
    anisotropy=None,
    domains=None,
    domain_column=None,
    progress=True,
)

Summary of n realizations, each seeded from seed and its index, the same for any number of threads.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default targets BlockModel

Regular or masked grid; one category per row.

required n int

Realizations.

100 seed int

Seed of the realizations.

0 keep bool or sequence of int

Realizations to return beside the summary.

None soft sequence of str or array_like

Soft probabilities: one column of targets per category, in code order, or an (n_targets, k) array. Each row is rescaled to sum 1; a row of nulls or NaN leaves its target without soft information. They combine with the image's probabilities by permanence of ratios, P(c) ∝ P_ti(c) * P_soft(c) / P0(c) (Journel, 2002), where P0 is the image's proportions, or the target proportions while the servosystem is on, so soft probabilities equal to P0 change nothing. Where the image and the soft probabilities share no category, shorter data events are tried. Hard data override them.

None anisotropy LocalAnisotropy

Turns and stretches the patterns at each target, taken from its nearest location. At angles 0 the image's y axis runs north, along the major axis, its x axis east, against the semi-major axis, and its z axis up, along the minor axis; the angles (azimuth clockwise from north, dip positive down, rake; azimuth only on a grid one cell thick) turn them as they turn a variogram. The image's structures grow by scale along its y axis, scale * semi_ratio along x and scale * minor_ratio along z: ratios and scales of 1 turn the patterns only. The image's cells are taken to have the size of the targets' cells. Angles and affinities are rounded by angle_step, and a template cell at grid offset g, on every multigrid level, reads the image at round(M g) for the matrix M of the target's class.

None domains array_like or label

Domain of each target, picking its training image when ti was a dict; every domain needs an image.

None domain_column str

Column of targets holding the domains, instead of domains.

None progress bool

Show a progress bar.

True

Returns:

Type Description CategoricalSummary or SimulationSummary

Probabilities, most likely category and entropy per target for a categorical training image; mean and variance per target for a continuous one.

Raises:

Type Description InvalidInput

If targets is not a regular or masked BlockModel, the search trees would not fit in memory (widen angle_step, lower template_size), soft is given with a continuous image or is not (n_targets, k) of non-negative values, some row mixing numbers and NaN or holding only zeros, or the domains do not match the training images.

docs.title: ImageQuilting
docs.text:
Image quilting: realizations pasted together from patches of a training image (Efros and Freeman, 2001; Mariethoz and Lefebvre, 2014).

Overlapping patches cover the targets along a raster path, x fastest, then y, then z. Each patch is drawn at random among the n_best positions of the training image that best match what the targets already hold under it: the cells of earlier patches, and the hard data weighted by data_weight. It joins the earlier patches along the seam where the two differ least: a minimum-error boundary cut in 2D, a graph cut in 3D (Kwatra et al., 2003). Positions whose patch holds a null of the training image are never pasted. Hard data steer the choice and are never pasted over.

The mismatch of a cell is 0 or 1 for codes, and the squared difference over the squared value range of the training image for values.

Two more kinds of data steer the choice when simulate is given them. Soft probabilities of each code at the targets add soft_weight times the mean of 1 - P(c) over the patch, c the code the patch puts in a block. A secondary variable known over both the training image and the targets, such as seismic amplitude, adds secondary_weight times the mean squared difference between the two over the patch, over the squared range of the training image's secondary column. A patch that compares many cells has its costs computed by FFT, with the same realizations.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default ti BlockModel

Regular or masked training image. Patterns are read in cell index space, so its origin, cell size and rotation play no part.

required column str

The float column of ti to copy.

required patch_size int or sequence of int

Cells of a patch along x, y and z (one int for all), clamped to the training image and to the targets.

40 overlap int or sequence of int

Cells a patch shares with the one before it along each axis, at most half the patch; by default a sixth of the patch, at least 1.

required n_best int

How many of the cheapest positions a patch is drawn from.

10 data_weight float

Weight of the hard data against the overlap in the choice of a patch; 0 leaves them out of it.

5.0 categorical bool

Whether the column holds codes (categories 0 to 254) or continuous values. By default it is categorical when every value is an integer from 0 to 254; set False for integer-valued continuous variables.

required secondary str

The float column of ti holding the secondary variable; simulate then needs it at the targets.

required secondary_weight float

Weight of the secondary variable against the overlap.

1.0 soft_weight float

Weight of the soft probabilities against the overlap.

1.0

Examples:

>>> grid = cs.BlockModel((0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1), (100, 100, 1))
>>> ti = cs.object_training_image(
...     grid, [{"shape": "channel", "code": 1, "proportion": 0.3, "width": 6}], seed=1
... )
>>> targets = cs.BlockModel((0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1), (80, 80, 1))
>>> summary = cs.ImageQuilting(ti, "facies", patch_size=20).simulate(targets, n=10)

Statistics of a block model against the data it was estimated from, per domain and over all.

Domain column of both model and data, or one name for each.

None

docs.title: classify
docs.text:
classify(
    criteria,
    rules,
    *,
    default="unclassified",
    domains=None,
    domain_column=None,
) -> ndarray

Labels each block with the first rule whose conditions all hold.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default criteria Table or dict of str to array_like

Per-block metrics, e.g. slope, efficiency from predict(..., diagnostics=True), nearest_dist, n_holes from neighborhood_stats and distances from hole_distance.

required rules sequence of (str, dict), or dict of domain to such a sequence

(label, {metric: (op, threshold)}) in priority order; op is one of <, <=, >, >=. NaN never satisfies a condition. With domains, a dict gives each domain its own rules; the None key covers domains not listed, and blocks of other domains get default.

required default str

Label where no rule holds.

'unclassified' domains array_like

Domain of each block, the keys of rules.

None domain_column str

The column of criteria holding the domains; instead of domains.

None

Examples:

>>> classify(d, [("measured", {"slope": (">=", 0.8), "n_holes": (">=", 3)}),
...              ("indicated", {"slope": (">=", 0.5)})], default="inferred")

docs.title: glossary
docs.text:
short definitions of the terms these pages use. elsewhere, hover a dotted term to see its definition.

angular tolerancethe half-angle of the cone around a direction within which pairs count toward a directional variogram. anisotropycontinuity that depends on direction, with a longer range along some directions than others. anisotropy ellipsethe ellipse, or ellipsoid in 3D, whose axes are the variogram ranges in the principal directions. arrowa standard in-memory column format that polars, pandas and pyarrow read directly. azimutha horizontal direction in degrees, measured clockwise from north. back-transformthe inverse of a transform, returning simulated scores to the original units. block krigingkriging of the average value over a block instead of the value at a point. boundary edgea mesh edge used by only one triangle, the rim of a hole. coefficient of variationthe standard deviation divided by the mean, a unitless measure of spread. collarthe point where a drill hole starts at the surface, with its coordinates and total length. compositea drill-hole interval of fixed length whose grade is the sampled-length-weighted mean of the assays it covers. compositesdrill-hole intervals of fixed length whose grades are the sampled-length-weighted means of the assays they cover. conditional biasa systematic error that depends on the estimate itself, with high estimates too high and low ones too low. contained metaltonnes × mean grade above a cutoff: the amount of metal the resource holds. cross-validationre-estimating each sample from the other samples and comparing the estimates with the actual values. CRScoordinate reference system: the named map projection or local grid the coordinates refer to. cutoffthe grade below which a block does not pay to mine; you report resources above it. declusteringweighting samples by the area or volume each represents, to correct statistics for clustered sampling. declustering effectthe sharing of weight among clustered samples, which kriging treats almost as one. degenerate facea triangle with a repeated corner or zero area. desurveyingturning a hole's collar and downhole survey angles into 3D coordinates along the hole. dipthe angle in degrees below the horizontal; positive points down. discretizationsplitting a block into a regular grid of points to measure what fraction lies inside a solid. domaina volume of rock whose values you treat as one population, such as one lithology or one vein. E-typethe mean of the realizations at each node, a smooth estimate comparable to kriging. experimental variogramhalf the mean squared difference between samples, computed for pairs grouped by lag. grade-tonnage curvetonnage and mean grade above each cutoff. grade–tonnage curvetonnes and mean grade above each cutoff, read as a curve over the cutoffs. h-scatterplota plot of the value at one end of each pair of samples a lag h apart against the value at the other end. inverse distancean estimator that weights each sample by a power of the inverse of its distance to the target. kriging efficiencyshare of the block variance an estimate resolves: 1 for a perfectly known block, 0 or less for one known no better than the mean. kriging variancethe error variance kriging predicts at a target, from the sample layout and the variogram alone. lagthe separation vector between two samples, a distance and a direction. lag tolerancehow far a pair's distance may differ from a lag center and still count toward that lag; half the lag spacing. misplaced volumelabeled volume outside its solid plus solid volume outside its labeled blocks. non-manifold edgea mesh edge shared by three or more triangles. normal scoresvalues replaced by the standard gaussian values with the same cumulative probability. nuggetvariogram value just above zero lag: variability at scales shorter than the closest samples, plus measurement error. ordinary krigingkriging with an unknown mean that is constant near the target; its weights sum to one. outliera value far from the rest of the distribution, often real but with outsized influence. parent blocka block of the regular grid a sub-blocked model starts from. parquetan open, compressed file format for tables that most data tools read. partial blocka block that a solid's surface crosses, so it lies partly inside and partly outside. positive definiteproperty of a variogram model that guarantees a positive variance for any weighted combination of samples. preferential samplingsampling that places more samples in some zones, usually the rich ones, than in others. random paththe random order in which sequential simulation visits the grid nodes. rangethe lag at which the variogram reaches its sill; beyond it, samples are uncorrelated. realizationone simulated map that honors the samples and reproduces the histogram and variogram of the data. realizationssimulated maps, each honoring the samples and reproducing the histogram and variogram of the data. screen effectthe loss of weight by a sample hidden behind a closer sample in the same direction. seedthe number that starts the random-number generator, so the same seed gives the same realizations. sentinela placeholder number such as -999 that a file uses to mark a missing value. SGSsequential gaussian simulation: it visits the nodes in random order, krigs each one, draws from the gaussian that kriging gives and adds the draw to the data. sillthe plateau of the variogram, reached when samples lie too far apart to be related. skewnessa measure of the asymmetry of a distribution; positive when a long tail runs to high values. slope of regressionthe slope of the true values regressed on the estimates; 1 means no conditional bias. smoothingthe loss of variance in an estimate, which averages neighboring samples and so varies less than the true grades. solida closed triangle mesh that bounds a volume, such as an ore body or a vein. solidsclosed triangle meshes that each bound a volume, such as ore bodies or veins. sub-blocka smaller cell a parent block is split into where a contact crosses it. sub-blockssmaller cells a parent block is split into where a contact crosses it. sub-cellone cell of the regular sub-grid inside a parent block; neighbors with one label merge into a sub-block. supportthe volume a value represents: a point, a length of core or a block. swath plotmean grade of blocks and samples in parallel slices along one direction, to find local bias. top cuta cap: values above it are set to it, to limit the influence of a few extreme values. value objectan object that holds model parameters and no data, such as a variogram or a search; it never changes after you build it. variogram mapthe experimental variogram computed for every direction and lag, drawn as an image. volume-variance effectaveraging values over larger supports keeps their mean and reduces their variance. windingthe order of a triangle's corners; counter-clockwise seen from outside makes its normal point out. wireframea triangle mesh drawn as its edges; a closed one is a solid.
